title: Don't Stop Teaching Comprehension--Just Embed It in Content
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler argues that comprehension skills and strategies are usually taught in isolation from content, in a reading class on disconnected topics, and that this standard approach has not raised reading scores. Drawing on Timothy Shanahan's observation that skills like finding the main idea collapse when texts get hard, she suggests treating them as habits worth trying rather than as transferable skills. She then marshals studies in which strategy instruction embedded in social studies content improved comprehension, and one in which poor readers learned strategies more easily using baseball stories because familiar content freed cognitive capacity. She adds that content-linked writing instruction can also build the knowledge and familiarity with written language that comprehension needs. Her closing analogy is that research designed around decontextualised instruction can mislead, like the medical theories that overlooked mosquitoes.
points: Skills such as finding the main idea behave less like transferable skills and more like habits that help only when students already understand the text.
Studies of seventh-graders and of English learners show that strategies taught within social studies content improve both content comprehension and strategy use.
Students learn strategies more easily in a subject they already know, consistent with cognitive load theory, as shown by the baseball-stories study.
Writing-strategy instruction tied to curriculum content and starting at the sentence level builds both writing and reading comprehension.
The evidence for isolated strategy teaching may reflect how studies were designed rather than what works best, and the cost has been the squeezing out of social studies and science.
quotes: The supposed comprehension skills that schools spend many hours on every week range from “finding the main idea” to “comparing and contrasting” to “determining the author’s purpose.” But one study showed that students had no trouble applying these kinds of skills to texts that were easy. When a text was difficult

Rather than thinking of things like “finding the main idea” as “skills,” it would make more sense to view them as habits: they won’t work in all situations, but it’s not a bad idea to have students remember to give them a try.

But skills and strategies are almost always taught in isolation from content, in a “reading” class. The topics of the readings are disconnected—the solar system today, sea mammals tomorrow—because the goal is that students learn the skill or strategy rather than any particular content.

All the students who felt that way remembered one or more steps of the strategy, 95% remembered two or more steps, and 73% remembered all the steps. Those results came after only twenty minutes of strategy instruction on each of three days.

The reason, researchers hypothesized, is that when kids are reading about a topic they’re familiar with, they have more cognitive capacity available to acquire the strategies—a conclusion that aligns well with general theories about cognitive load.

As with strategy instruction explicitly focused on reading, writing-strategy instruction that is linked to specific content can build the knowledge that is an essential component of comprehension. It’s also a powerful way of familiarizing students with the conventions of written language, another necessity.

Relying on those studies alone to say that’s the best way to do it—and to do it day after day, year after year, in a world where such instruction has virtually eliminated social studies and science in many schools—makes no sense.
